title: Malachi
subtitle: All Four Chapters - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Messianic Connections (WEB)

items.value: This book walks through all four chapters of Malachi, one chapter at a time, with the full text of every chapter printed in it. It grew out of a Saturday study group working through the Bible book by book, and it is the third volume in this series.

Malachi is short enough to read in a single sitting - fifty-five verses, less than five pages in most Bibles. That is part of why it gets skipped. It sits at the back of the Old Testament like an appendix, and a great many people who have read Genesis several times have never read this at all. It repays the twenty minutes many times over.
It is a companion to the Jeremiah and Matthew volumes in this series, and it is built the same way. If you have used either of those, everything here will be familiar.

The prose is the point. The tables and footnotes are apparatus - useful, and worth using - but they exist to serve a reading of Malachi, not to replace one. If you only ever read the chapter introductions and the scripture text, you will have read this book properly.

sections.heading: How this book is put together

items.value: Every chapter follows the same shape.

values: **Key Notes** - the observations worth having in hand before you read: a word that carries more than the translation shows, a custom the first readers took for granted, a connection to something earlier in the book. Each note ends with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - eight passages that stand behind or alongside the chapter, grouped by theme.
**Messianic Connections** - six or seven places where the chapter points forward to Messiah. Malachi carries a remarkable number of these for its length, and they are explained further below.
**For Further Study** - three places to go deeper, from three different traditions.
**Introduction** - the chapter read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The chapter itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

items.value: Every scripture reference in the book is a live link to the World English Bible on BibleGateway. In the interactive edition, hovering over a footnote marker shows the full text of the passages cited and a line on why they connect, so you can follow a cross-reference without losing your place.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this book uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah, as the group this material was written for does.

The printed scripture text is never altered. The World English Bible renders the covenant name as Yahweh already, so in Malachi the notes and the text mostly agree - which is not the case in the Matthew volume, where the printed text reads Jesus throughout. Everything stands exactly as the translators set it.

sections.heading: A note on the chapter titles

items.value: The chapter titles in this book are not traditional and are not found in any Bible. They were written for this study - they name what struck us in that chapter rather than summarising it. Nobody should take them as headings the text itself supplies.

The name means "my messenger," and that is either a very fitting name for a prophet or not a name at all. Some ancient readers took it as a title rather than a person - the Septuagint translators seem to have read it that way, and the Targum attributed the book to Ezra. Nothing else about the man is recorded: no father named, no home town, no king's reign to date him by. The book gives you a voice and nothing else.

The date is easier, and it is fixed by internal evidence rather than by a heading. There is a temple, and sacrifices are being offered in it (1:10, 3:10), so this is after the rebuilding finished in 516 BC. There is a **governor** rather than a king (1:8), using the Persian loanword *pechah* - so Judah is a province of the Persian empire, not a kingdom. And the sins the book attacks are the same ones Nehemiah found and fought: a corrupted priesthood, marriages to foreign wives, and tithes withheld from the Levites.

That puts Malachi around 430 BC, give or take a decade - roughly a hundred years after the first exiles came home. It is the last prophetic voice in the Hebrew canon, and after it comes four centuries of silence.
You cannot read Malachi properly without understanding the mood he is speaking into, because the mood is the whole problem.

Haggai and Zechariah had promised extraordinary things. The glory of this latter house would be greater than the former. Nations would come. A branch would build the temple and bear royal honour. The people who heard those promises rebuilt the temple on the strength of them.

Then a century passed. The temple was modest. There was no king - just a Persian appointee. The nations had not come. Life was ordinary, the harvests were unremarkable, and the enormous promises had not arrived. Nobody had renounced the faith. They simply stopped expecting anything from it, and worship became something you got through rather than something you meant.
That is the condition Malachi addresses, and it is why the book still lands. It is not written to people in open rebellion. It is written to people who still show up.

Malachi has a structure unlike any other prophet, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. The book is a series of arguments, and each one runs the same three steps: God makes an assertion, the people answer back with a question, and God responds at length.
There are six or seven of these depending on how you count, and the people's questions are the hinge of each one:

Notice what all seven have in common. Every one is a denial, and every one is sincere. These people genuinely do not think they are guilty of what they are being charged with. That is the most uncomfortable thing about the book - not that the people are wicked, but that they cannot see it, and are quite willing to argue the point with God.
For its length, Malachi carries an unusual weight of forward-looking material, and the New Testament draws on it heavily.

Two messengers appear in 3:1, and they are not the same one. There is a messenger who prepares the way, and there is the Lord who suddenly comes to His temple - called in the same breath the messenger of the covenant. All four Gospels apply the first of these to John the Baptist, and Yahshua Himself does so explicitly (Matthew 11:10). The Elijah promise that closes the book at 4:5-6 is the same figure named a second time, and it is the last thing the Old Testament says.

Alongside those, the book gives us the refiner's fire, the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings, the pure offering made among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting, and the book of remembrance written for those who feared Yahweh. The second table in each chapter follows these forward, as the Jeremiah volume does.

The last word in the Hebrew Bible's prophetic section is a curse - "lest I come and strike the earth with a curse." Ancient readers found that hard. The custom in synagogue reading is to go back and repeat verse 5 after verse 6, so the reading does not finish on that word, and the Greek translators reversed the final two verses to the same effect.

It is worth sitting with rather than softening. The book ends on a condition, not a verdict - hearts turned, or a land struck. And then nothing, for four hundred years, until a man appears in the wilderness dressed like Elijah and the argument resumes.

Malachi can be read in one sitting, and at least once it should be - straight through, all four chapters, before any of the apparatus. The disputations build on each other and the shape only shows at speed.
After that, take a chapter at a time. Read the introduction first, then the chapter itself, and come back to the notes and tables afterward; they will mean more once the text is in you.
If you are reading with others, the introductions are written to be read aloud. That is what they were for originally, and they still work best that way.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 1 - I Have Loved You, and a Table They Called Contemptible
chapters.title: I Have Loved You, and a Table They Called Contemptible
keyNotes: The name Malachi means "my messenger," and it may be a title rather than a name. Nothing else about the man is recorded - no father, no home town, no king to date him by (Malachi 1:1).
"A revelation" translates massa, which also means a burden - something lifted and carried (Malachi 1:1).
The book is built as a series of disputes. God asserts, the people answer with a question, God responds. Seven of those questions run through the book, and the first arrives in verse 2 (Malachi 1:2).
"How have you loved us?" is not sarcasm. It is the honest question of people a hundred years into a restoration that never became what the prophets promised (Malachi 1:2).
The answer is not a list of blessings but a fact of election, and it goes back to the womb - the older will serve the younger (Malachi 1:2, Genesis 25:23).
"Esau I hated" is covenant language, not emotion. The same Hebrew verb describes Leah being "hated" in a household where she was in fact the less-loved wife, not a despised one (Malachi 1:3).
Edom's confidence that they will simply rebuild is exactly what Obadiah had said would fail (Malachi 1:4).
The argument to the priests begins from the ordinary world: a son honors his father, a servant his master. Nobody disputes that part (Malachi 1:6).
"How have we despised your name?" - they do not know they are doing it. That is the point of the whole book (Malachi 1:6).
The law was explicit that a blemished animal was not acceptable, so this is not ignorance; it is calculation (Malachi 1:8, Leviticus 22:20-22).
"Present it now to your governor" is a devastating test, and the word governor is the Persian loanword pechah - which is how we know roughly when this was written (Malachi 1:8).
"Oh that there were one among you who would shut the doors" - God says closed would be better than this. Not everything offered as worship is received as worship (Malachi 1:10).

Verse 11 is startling in its reach: from the rising of the sun to its setting, among the nations, a pure offering. Said to a small province that thought it was the only place God had left (Malachi 1:11).
"Yahweh's table" is the altar. Calling it contemptible is a verdict on the One who eats there (Malachi 1:7, 12).
"What a weariness" - the word carries the sense of drudgery, hardship, a chore. They were bored (Malachi 1:13).
The deceiver in verse 14 is precise: he has a sound male in his flock, vows it, and then substitutes the defective one. He is not poor. He is cheap (Malachi 1:14).
"I am a great King" borrows the Persian emperor's own title and puts it where it belongs (Malachi 1:14).

intro: The first thing to establish about Malachi is who is being addressed, because everything in the book depends on it. These are not pagans or idolaters. They are the people who came home. Their grandparents returned from Babylon, rebuilt the temple, restarted the sacrifices, and waited for what Haggai and Zechariah had promised.

It did not come. A century passed. The temple was modest. There was no king, only a Persian appointee. The nations had not streamed in. Nobody renounced the faith - they simply stopped expecting anything from it, and worship became a routine rather than an expectation.

So the opening exchange is not defiance. When God says I have loved you and the people answer how, that is a hundred years of quiet disappointment finally spoken aloud. And the answer is worth noticing: not a catalogue of recent mercies, but a return to the womb. Two brothers, one chosen, and the choice made before either had done anything at all.

The address then turns to the priests, and the argument becomes specific. It begins from common ground that nobody will contest - a son honors his father, a servant his master - and then asks the obvious question. Where is mine?

Their reply is the recurring note of the book: how have we despised your name? They do not know. That is what makes this uncomfortable rather than merely severe. The blemished animals had become normal. Nobody had decided to insult God; the standard slid, one defensible compromise at a time, until a sick lamb on the altar looked like nothing at all.

Then the line that closes the argument. Offer it to the governor. Take the animal you have just judged good enough for God and present it to the Persian official as tax, and see whether he accepts it.
Verse 10 follows, and it is among the hardest sentences in the prophets: I wish someone would shut the doors. Not reform the service - end it. God would rather receive nothing than receive this.

Yet verse 11 sits in the middle of the rebuke and is enormous. From the rising of the sun to its setting, among the nations, a pure offering. A small, discouraged province in a corner of the Persian empire is told that the name it has been treating carelessly will be great everywhere - with them or without them.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 2 - The Covenant of Levi, and the Wife of Your Youth
chapters.title: The Covenant of Levi, and the Wife of Your Youth
keyNotes: "Now, you priests, this commandment is for you" - the address narrows. Chapter 1 accused; chapter 2 sentences (Malachi 2:1).
The curse falls on their blessings, which is exact retribution: pronouncing the blessing was the priest's defining task (Malachi 2:2, Numbers 6:23-27).
"I have cursed them already" - the judgment is not pending. It has been in effect while they carried on (Malachi 2:2).
The dung of the festival sacrifices was carried outside the camp and burned. Spread on their faces, it puts the priest where the refuse goes (Malachi 2:3, Leviticus 4:11-12).
The covenant with Levi is most likely the covenant of peace given to Phinehas, who acted when no one else would (Malachi 2:4-5, Numbers 25:12-13).
"Life and peace" describes what the priesthood was for before it describes what it lost (Malachi 2:5).
"The law of truth was in his mouth" - the priest's first job was teaching, not sacrificing (Malachi 2:6, Leviticus 10:11).
"He turned many away from iniquity" is the measure of a true priest, and it is a startling standard (Malachi 2:6).
"He is the messenger of Yahweh of Armies" uses the same word as the book's own title. The priests were malakim, and had stopped carrying the message (Malachi 2:7).
"You have caused many to stumble in the law" - the charge is not that they broke it but that they made others break it (Malachi 2:8).
At verse 10 the address widens from priests to everyone, and the tone changes from verdict to appeal (Malachi 2:10).
"Don't we all have one father?" is deliberately ambiguous - Abraham, or God as creator. The argument works either way (Malachi 2:10).
"Married the daughter of a foreign god" is the same crisis Ezra and Nehemiah confronted, and it is framed as a religious act, not an ethnic one (Malachi 2:11, Nehemiah 13:23-27).
The altar is covered with tears - the weeping of discarded wives, or the useless weeping of men whose offerings are not received. The Hebrew allows both, and both are terrible (Malachi 2:13).
"Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth" makes marriage a covenant with a third party present, not a private arrangement (Malachi 2:14).
Verse 15 is the most difficult verse in the book to translate; every English version handles it differently. What survives every reading is the reason given: He sought godly offspring (Malachi 2:15).
"Take heed to your spirit" is said twice in two verses. The problem starts inside, before anything is done (Malachi 2:15-16).
Verse 17 opens the fourth dispute and properly belongs with chapter 3 - the complaint about God's justice is what 3:1 answers (Malachi 2:17).

intro: Chapter 1 was the accusation; chapter 2 is the sentence, and the priests are still in the dock. The punishment fits with terrible precision - I will curse your blessings. Consider what a priest did: he blessed people. Yahweh bless you and keep you. That was the office. And God says the one thing they exist to do is being turned against them.

Verse 3 is among the most graphic images in the prophets. The dung of your feasts, on your faces. When a sacrifice was offered the offal was carried outside the camp and burned as refuse. The sentence is a matched one: they have treated the altar as a rubbish heap, so they will be put where the rubbish goes.

Then, unexpectedly, comes a description of what a priest was meant to be, and it is beautiful. My covenant with him was life and peace. The law of truth was in his mouth. He walked with me. He turned many away from iniquity. That is the standard - not correct performance of ritual, but people turned around.

Verse 7 carries a word worth pausing on. The priest is the messenger of Yahweh of Armies - malak, the same word as the name on the front of the book. Every one of these men was a Malachi, and they had stopped carrying anything.
At verse 10 the address widens to everyone, and the charge is treachery, the same word four times over: against one another, against the covenant of the fathers, against wives.

Verse 13 needs care. The altar is covered with tears - and the Hebrew permits two readings. They may be the tears of women who have been put away, or the useless tears of men who cannot understand why their offerings are refused. Both are devastating, and the point is the same either way: God knows what is happening in the house, and it is why He will not receive what is brought to the temple.
Verse 14 reframes the subject entirely. Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth. That is not an agreement between two people. It is a covenant with a third party present.

Verse 15 is the hardest verse in the book to render; three translations will give three different sentences. But one clause survives every reading - He sought godly offspring - and it names what is actually at stake. Not only the happiness of two adults, but the generation after them.
And twice in two verses: take heed to your spirit. Not to conduct. To the spirit. It begins inside, long before anything is done.

verses.1: “Now, you priests, this commandment is for you.

verses.11: Judah has dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah has profaned the holiness of Yahweh which he loves, and has married the daughter of a foreign god.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 3 - Two Messengers, a Refiner's Fire, and a Book of Remembrance
chapters.title: Two Messengers, a Refiner's Fire, and a Book of Remembrance
keyNotes: "My messenger" is mal'aki - the book's own name appears as a common noun in its most famous verse (Malachi 3:1).
There are two distinct figures in verse 1, and possibly three: the messenger who prepares the way, the Lord who suddenly comes to His temple, and the messenger of the covenant (Malachi 3:1).
"The Lord whom you seek" answers the complaint that just closed chapter 2 - where is the God of justice? He is coming, and that turns out not to be a comfortable answer (Malachi 2:17, 3:1).
"Suddenly" is pith'om, used of things that arrive without warning. The temple He comes to is His own (Malachi 3:1).
Two cleaning images follow, and both are violent. A refiner's fire melts; fullers' soap was harsh alkali, and the cloth was beaten (Malachi 3:2).
"He will sit as a refiner" - the refiner does not leave the crucible. The silver is watched the whole time it is in the fire (Malachi 3:3).
The first people purified are the sons of Levi - the very priests condemned in chapter 2. The judgment is aimed at restoration, not disposal (Malachi 3:3).
The list in verse 5 moves from the obviously religious to the obviously social, and God calls Himself a swift witness against both (Malachi 3:5).
Withholding a labourer's wages sits in the same list as sorcery and adultery (Malachi 3:5).
"For I, Yahweh, don't change; therefore you are not consumed" - the unchangeableness of God is offered here as the reason Israel still exists, not as an abstraction (Malachi 3:6).
"Return to me, and I will return to you" is met with "How shall we return?" - they cannot identify anything to repent of (Malachi 3:7).
"Will a man rob God?" uses a rare verb that carries the sense of defrauding or taking by stealth (Malachi 3:8).
The charge is tithes and offerings - both the required portion and the voluntary one (Malachi 3:8).
"Test me now in this" is the one place in Scripture where God invites a test of Himself (Malachi 3:10).
"The devourer" is most likely locusts or blight - the ordinary agricultural disasters of that country (Malachi 3:11).
The seventh dispute is the bleakest: it is vain to serve God. Not that He does not exist - that He does not pay (Malachi 3:14).
"Walked mournfully" describes the dress and bearing of mourners; they had been going through penitential motions and resenting it (Malachi 3:14).
The book of remembrance reflects a real Persian court practice - a chronicle of services done for the king, read back to him (Malachi 3:16, Esther 6:1).
What gets written down is not a great work. It is people who feared Yahweh talking to each other (Malachi 3:16).
"My own possession" is segullah, the treasured personal property of a king - the word used at Sinai (Malachi 3:17, Exodus 19:5).

intro: Chapter 2 closed with a complaint - where is the God of justice? Chapter 3 opens with the answer, and the answer is that He is on His way. Which is what was asked for, and not at all what was wanted.

Verse 1 is among the most quoted verses in the Old Testament, and there are at least two figures in it. Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me - that is one. And the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple - that is another. All four Gospels apply the first to John the Baptist, and Yahshua states plainly that this is who it was.

Two pictures of what that coming accomplishes follow, and neither is gentle. A refiner's fire, and fullers' soap. Refining means melting - the ore is destroyed as ore in order to release the silver. Fullers' soap was harsh alkali, and the cloth soaked in it was then beaten. Both images are about getting something out of something else, and both are painful.

But verse 3 rewards close reading. He will sit as a refiner. The silversmith does not put metal in the fire and walk away; left too long it is ruined. He stays, watching, the whole time it is in the heat.
And the first to be refined are the sons of Levi - the very priests condemned throughout chapter 2. The fire is not there to dispose of them. It is there to give them their office back.

Verse 5 deserves attention for its list. Sorcerers, adulterers, perjurers - and then those who oppress the hired worker in his wages, the widow, the fatherless, the foreigner. Underpaying a labourer appears in the same sentence as sorcery, and God names Himself a swift witness against all of it.
Then: return to me, and I will return to you. And the reply is how? They cannot identify anything to repent of. So the answer is given, and it is money. You are robbing me.
Here too is the one place in Scripture where God invites a test of Himself. Bring the tithe and see what I will do. Nowhere else is that offered.

But the verse that lingers is 16, and it is quiet. After all the argument, some who feared Yahweh spoke with one another. That is all they did. They talked. And God stopped, and listened, and had it written in a book. Not a great work, not a reform movement - a conversation between people who still cared, entered into the record.

chapters.heading: CHAPTER 4 - The Sun of Righteousness and the Last Word of the Prophets
chapters.title: The Sun of Righteousness and the Last Word of the Prophets
keyNotes: "The day comes, it burns as a furnace" picks up the day named repeatedly in chapter 3 and brings it to its conclusion (Malachi 4:1).
"Neither root nor branch" is a total image drawn from farming - nothing left to grow back (Malachi 4:1).
The same fire that refines in 3:2-3 consumes here. What it does depends entirely on what it meets (Malachi 3:2, 4:1).
"The sun of righteousness" is a title found nowhere else in Scripture (Malachi 4:2).
"Wings" translates kanaph, which is also the word for the corner or hem of a garment - the part of the robe a desperate woman once reached for (Malachi 4:2).
Winged sun discs were a common royal emblem across that world, including on Persian and Judean seals; the image would have been immediately familiar (Malachi 4:2).
"Leap like calves of the stall" is the picture of an animal let out of the pen after being shut in - relief and undignified joy (Malachi 4:2).
"Remember the law of Moses" is the closing instruction, and Horeb is named - the mountain where it was given (Malachi 4:4).
Moses and Elijah are named together in the last three verses of the Old Testament. Both met God at Horeb, and both appear together once more on a mountain (Malachi 4:4-5).
The Elijah promise is the same figure as the messenger of 3:1, named a second time and given a name (Malachi 3:1, 4:5).
"Before the great and terrible day" places this ahead of judgment, not after it (Malachi 4:5).
"Turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" is quoted over John the Baptist before he is born (Malachi 4:6, Luke 1:17).
The final word is a curse - cherem, the term for something devoted to destruction. The book ends on a condition rather than a verdict (Malachi 4:6).
Ancient synagogue practice repeats verse 5 after verse 6 so the reading does not end on that word, and the Greek translators reversed the last two verses for the same reason (Malachi 4:5-6).
After this, no prophetic voice is recorded for roughly four centuries - until a man appears in the wilderness dressed like Elijah (Malachi 4:5).

intro: Four chapters, and this is the end - not only of Malachi but of the Old Testament. What follows is roughly four centuries with no prophetic voice on record.

It opens with fire: the day comes, burning like a furnace. Hold that next to 3:2, one chapter earlier, where there was also fire - a refiner's fire that purified the sons of Levi. The same fire, and an entirely different outcome. What it does depends on what it meets.
Then verse 2, one of the loveliest sentences in the prophets. To you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings. The title appears nowhere else in Scripture.

The word rendered wings is kanaph, which also means the corner, edge or hem of a garment - worth remembering when reading of a woman who had bled for twelve years and thought that touching the edge of a robe would be enough.
And the response of the healed is undignified. They leap like calves of the stall: a young animal shut in through the winter, and the gate finally opened.

The last three verses name two men. Remember the law of Moses. And, behold, I will send you Elijah. Both met God at Horeb; and centuries later, on another mountain in front of three frightened fishermen, these are precisely the two who appear.

The Elijah promise concerns families - hearts of fathers turned to children, and children to fathers. When Gabriel stands in the temple and tells an old priest he will have a son, this is the verse he quotes.

And then it stops. The final word of the Old Testament is curse, and it troubled ancient readers enough that synagogue practice repeats verse 5 afterwards so the reading does not end there, while the Greek translators reversed the final two verses to the same end.

But the sentence should not be softened too quickly, because of what it actually says: lest I come and strike the earth with a curse. Lest. It is a condition, not a verdict. The Old Testament does not close with sentence passed. It closes with a door left open, and then silence - until a man walks out of the wilderness dressed like Elijah, and the conversation resumes exactly where it stopped.

verses.1: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
verses.2: But to you who fear my name shall the sun of righteousness arise with healing in its wings. You will go out, and leap like calves of the stall.

verses.5: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
verses.6: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”

cites.text: Therefore the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will send among his fat ones leanness; and under his glory a burning will be kindled like the burning of fire. The light of Israel will be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame; and it will burn and devour his thorns and his briers in one day.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.

1.why: a burning like the burning of fire, and a day that comes as a thief

cites.text: Yet I destroyed the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.
“Even now the ax lies at the root of the trees. Therefore every tree that doesn’t produce good fruit is cut down, and cast into the fire.

1.why: destroyed his fruit above and his roots beneath, and an axe already at the root

cites.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the dawn from on high will visit us, to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death; to guide our feet into the way of peace.”

2.why: people walking in darkness who saw a great light, and the sunrise from on high

cites.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
Behold, a woman who had an issue of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.”

2.why: by his wounds we are healed, and a woman who only wanted to touch the hem

cites.text: He will cover you with his feathers. Under his wings you will take refuge. His faithfulness is your shield and rampart.
Behold, a woman who had an issue of blood for twelve years came behind him, and touched the fringe of his garment; for she said within herself, “If I just touch his garment, I will be made well.”

2.why: covered under his wings, and the corner of a garment reached for in a crowd

cites.text: For he has brought down those who dwell on high, the lofty city. He lays it low. He lays it low even to the ground. He brings it even to the dust. The foot shall tread it down; Even the feet of the poor, and the steps of the needy.”
And the God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

3.why: the lofty city trodden down by the feet of the poor, and Satan crushed under yours

cites.text: The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in which the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will be dissolved with fervent heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.

3.why: before the great and awesome day, and the day the elements dissolve

cites.text: the day that you stood before Yahweh your God in Horeb, when Yahweh said to me, “Assemble the people to me, and I will make them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me all the days that they live on the earth, and that they may teach their children.”

Only be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe to do according to all the law, which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.

4.why: the day they stood at Horeb, and the command not to turn from it right or left

cites.text: His disciples asked him, saying, “Then why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?” Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things, but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.” Then the disciples understood that he spoke to them of John the Baptizer.

He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, ‘to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children,’ and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to prepare a people prepared for the Lord.”

5.why: why then do the scribes say Elijah must come first - and the answer given at a cradle

cites.text: If you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah, who is to come.

Jesus answered them, “Elijah indeed comes first, and will restore all things, but I tell you that Elijah has come already, and they didn’t recognize him, but did to him whatever they wanted to. Even so the Son of Man will also suffer by them.”

5.why: if you are willing to receive it, this is Elijah who is to come

cites.text: He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord, their God. He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, ‘to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children,’ and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to prepare a people prepared for the Lord.”
Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart, and the heart of your offspring, to love Yahweh your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, that you may live.

6.why: turning the hearts of the fathers, and a heart circumcised so that you may live

cites.text: Men will dwell therein, and there will be no more curse; but Jerusalem will dwell safely.
There will be no curse any more. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will serve him.

6.why: there will be no more curse - the last word of the Old Testament answered in the last chapter of the New

parts.title: Major Themes Across Malachi 1-4
items: A book written to people who never left, and never expected anything again
Seven questions, every one a denial, and every one sincerely meant
Love proved by election rather than by circumstances
Worship God would rather not receive, and a door He would rather have shut
The slow slide: nobody decides to despise Him, the standard just moves
Offering God what you would be embarrassed to hand the tax official
A name great among the nations, announced to a province that thought it was the last one left
Priests who were messengers and stopped carrying the message
The blessing itself turned into a curse - exact retribution on the exact office
What a priest was supposed to be: life, peace, truth in the mouth, many turned from iniquity
Treachery at home as the reason offerings are refused at the temple
Marriage as a covenant with a witness standing in the room
Take heed to your spirit - said twice, because it starts inside
Where is the God of justice, and the discovery that He is on His way
Two messengers in one verse, and four hundred years between the promise and the voice
A refiner who sits down and does not leave the crucible
The condemned priesthood purified first
Underpaid wages in the same sentence as sorcery
I do not change - offered as the reason they still exist
The one invitation in Scripture to put God to the test
It is vain to serve God: the complaint the whole book is answering
A book of remembrance written for people who only talked to each other
The same fire that refines the silver burns the stubble
The sun of righteousness, and a hem reached for in a crowd
Moses and Elijah named together, and seen together on a mountain
An Old Testament that ends on a condition, not a verdict
